name: Global health systems unsuited to youth needs

content.text: The three-year-long review, published as a series of articles in the Journal of Adolescent Health, is written by eight AKU researchers alongside academics from Canada, Australia, India and the United Kingdom.

The Adolescent Health and Wellbeing: Current State of the Evidence authors assessed the performance of adolescent health initiatives around the world in six key areas and found that health systems in in rich, middle income and poor countries were more geared towards young children and adults rather than adolescents.

Adolescence is a critical stage of life accompanied by rapid physical, emotional and social development. The need for interventions to boost youth health is particularly important since one in four people around the world are between the ages of 10 and 24, and represent the future adult population - at a time of unparalleled economic and social change.

In 2012, 1.3 million young people lost their lives from preventable or treatable causes, "an unacceptable rate of mortality". The odds of dying as a young person are almost two times higher in South Asia and four times higher in sub-Saharan Africa than in other regions.

Speaking about the need to focus on adolescent health, Professor Zulfiqar Bhutta, Founding Director of the Aga Khan University's Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health and co-Director of the SickKids Centre for Global Child Health in Toronto, said: "Good adolescent health can result in a 'triple dividend' for society since healthy youngsters possess the physical and mental attributes to fully achieve their potential, live a healthier adult life and give birth to healthier children."

"Only by fully engaging and supporting young people can countries achieve their full economic potential. We need to understand the areas where interventions are working and highlight the areas where there are knowledge gaps, to deliver the knowledge that gives policymakers the evidence to enact change."

The review authors analysed programmes and interventions in the vital areas of immunisation, nutrition, mental health, substance abuse, sexual and reproductive health, and injury prevention. Worryingly, they noted a number of areas where no research was available to inform health policy and suggested new research strategies to meet these needs.

Immunisation programmes are not being evaluated and where they are, the focus is on young children rather than adolescents. There is a need for research on why adolescents miss being vaccinated and for integrated interventions where governments, schools and mobile healthcare workers can support the goal of protecting young people from preventable disease.

Reviews of nutrition programmes highlighted the severe problem of undernutrition, with pregnant adolescent still-growing girls most at risk. Encouragingly, micronutrient supplements are helping decrease the prevalence of anemia leading to better birth outcomes. The review authors also called on the academic community to pay greater attention to the problem of obesity in low and middle income countries and to investigate the association between better nutrition and improved learning skills and productivity

In the area of sexual and reproductive health, there are knowledge gaps on female genital mutilation, child marriage, and sexual and intimate partner violence. While there is evidence that sexual education programmes and contraceptive availability in youth-friendly settings is helping achieve health objectives, further work is needed to evaluate whether messages about sexual health and contraceptives aired through digital media are useful to young people.

Research on drug abuse found that school-based initiatives had delivered results but most studies centered on the use of cognitive behavioral therapy (where people are encouraged to change their thinking patterns about issues). Coordinated approaches that involved interventions via school and the family had shown promise, particularly in the case of smoking and a small effect in the case of alcohol misuse. They also highlighted the need for studies to report data on how interventions were affecting particular genders and socioeconomic subgroups.

Commenting on how to deliver improved adolescent health services, Professor Marleen Temmerman, Director of the Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health, East Africa, at AKU and a Senior Adviser to the World Health Organization on Women, Children and Adolescent Health, who co-authored the introduction to the study said: "Schools are an increasingly important platform for action. With a growing retention of adolescents in secondary education in so many countries, the task of developing and scaling-up health actions within schools should become a priority."

"In many contexts, community-based intervention is an effective alternative and likely to remain important in places where rates of secondary school attendance are low. The value of youth-friendly care is also clearer, particularly around sexual and reproductive health services. In addition, there are new platforms with great potential, none more so than social and digital media. With the rollout of broadband in many countries, there is an unprecedented opportunity for innovation and evaluation to extend our knowledge of digital media interventions," Professor Temmerman added.

Overall, researchers found a lack of studies in low and middle income countries. Across the board, they added that the success of interventions in girls as opposed to boys is often unclear, as is the scalability of interventions across socioeconomic, socially marginalised and ethnic groups.

The review was supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and involved AKU researchers Dr Ahmed Arshad, Dr Anadil Faqqah, Dr Jai Das, Marium Naveed Khan, Dr Mehar Hooda, Dr Nida Sajjad, Rehana Salam, Professor Zulfiqar Bhutta, with Dr Marleen Temmerman authoring the editorial introducing the series.

content.title: Global health systems unsuited to youth needs
content.author: Muhammad Altamash
content.description: Today with about 1.8 billion young people, the world's largest-ever generation of adolescents and young adults in human history, a global study has found health services for this group to be fragmented, poorly coordinated and uneven in quality, whilst improving their survival and wellbeing is critical for the success of the Sustainable Development Goals and a sustainable future.
